name: Annas
title: High Priest and influential leader of a priestly dynasty
summary: Annas was one of the most influential Jewish religious leaders in the first century. He was appointed high priest around 6 AD by the Roman governor Quirinius in Syria, and held the office formally until about 15 AD. Despite being deposed by the Romans, he continued to wield considerable power behind the scenes in Jewish society. His influence was so pervasive that five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas all served as high priests after him—a priestly dynasty without parallel in the Second Temple period. In the New Testament, Annas appears as a figure with real authority: Jesus was brought to him first after his arrest, before being sent on to Caiaphas. Luke mentions Annas and Caiaphas side by side as high priests, underscoring his continued status. After Pentecost, Annas was also present in the council that interrogated the apostles Peter and John. Rabbinic sources refer critically to his family’s exercise of power at key moments, and together the sources portray a powerful figure operating at the intersection of Jewish religion and Roman politics.

keyEvents.title: Annas mentioned as high priest alongside Caiaphas
keyEvents.description: Annas is named together with Caiaphas as high priest when God's word came to John the Baptist in the fifteenth year of Emperor Tiberius. The mention of two high priests at the same time is unusual and reflects Annas' continued religious and political influence even after his formal removal by the Romans.

keyEvents.title: Jesus is brought to Annas after his arrest
keyEvents.description: After Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, he was first taken to Annas, the father-in-law of the reigning high priest Caiaphas. The fact that Jesus was brought to Annas first shows that he was still regarded as the true power within the circle of high priests.

keyEvents.title: Annas interrogates Jesus
keyEvents.description: Annas questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered that he had always spoken openly and urged Annas to ask those who had heard him. One of the guards then struck Jesus for this answer, which was seen as disrespectful toward the high priest.

keyEvents.title: Annas sends Jesus on to Caiaphas
keyEvents.description: After the initial interrogation, Annas sent Jesus bound onward to the high priest Caiaphas for the formal trial before the Jewish council.

keyEvents.title: Annas in the council assembly against the apostles
keyEvents.description: After Pentecost, Peter and John were brought before the Jewish council. Annas was present, and the text refers to him with the title high priest – an expression of his enduring status – along with Caiaphas and others from the high-priestly family. They questioned the apostles about the healing of the lame man at the temple gate.

versions.summary: Annas (also called Hananiah) was a Jewish high priest from approximately 6 to 15 AD, appointed by the Roman legate Quirinius. Even after he was removed from office, he retained enormous political and religious influence, and five of his sons as well as his son-in-law Caiaphas served as high priests after him. He played a central role in the trial of Jesus and in the persecution of the early apostles.

versions.summary: Annas (Greek form of the Hebrew Hananiah) was the Jewish high priest from about 6 to 15 AD, appointed by the Roman legate Quirinius. Even after he was removed from office by the Romans, he retained enormous political and religious influence in the Jewish community. According to the historian Josephus, five of his sons as well as his son-in-law Caiaphas served as high priests after him, which testifies to the family's exceptional position of power. Annas played a central role in the trial of Jesus, who was first brought to him after his arrest, and he was also present when the Jewish council interrogated the apostles Peter and John after Pentecost.

footnotes.text: Annas (Greek: Ἅννας) is likely a shortened form of the Hebrew name Hananiah (חֲנַנְיָה), meaning 'the Lord is gracious.' The name appears in Greek form in the New Testament, reflecting the widespread Hellenization of Jewish names in the first century.

The Jewish historian Josephus (Ant. 18.2.1–2; 20.9.1) provides important additional information about Annas (Ananus). He was appointed high priest by Quirinius, the Roman legate of Syria, around 6 AD, and was deposed by Valerius Gratus around 15 AD. Josephus describes him as extremely fortunate because five of his sons—Eleazar, Jonathan, Theophilus, Matthias, and Annas the Younger—all became high priests after him. This priestly dynasty is unique in the Second Temple period.

Under Roman rule, the high priest was appointed and removed by the Roman authorities, breaking with the biblical tradition where the office of high priest was originally a lifelong position (Num 35:25). Even after his deposition, Annas continued to be recognized as high priest by many Jews, which explains why Luke mentions him alongside Caiaphas and why Jesus was first brought to him after his arrest.

Archaeological excavations in Jerusalem have uncovered numerous richly decorated burial chambers and ossuaries (bone boxes) from the first century belonging to high-priestly families. Although none of these are directly linked to Annas, they provide a picture of the immense wealth and power these families held. An inscription with the name 'Caiaphas' has also been found on an ossuary, closely linking the archaeological material to Annas's son-in-law.

In rabbinic literature (Talmud, Pesachim 57a), there are complaints about the high-priestly families and their abuse of power. The 'House of Hanin' (identified with Annas's family) is specifically mentioned for its whispering evil and violence against the people. This suggests that the family's negative reputation was well known in Jewish tradition and provides independent testimony to the power the family wielded.

The term 'high priest' is used in the New Testament in a broader sense than the strictly formal office. In Acts 4:6, Annas is called high priest even though he had formally been deposed. This extended usage reflects that in Jewish practice, the title could refer to someone who had held the office and still enjoyed its associated authority and recognition.
